purpose: Follow current predicate truths through an argument’s premises and conclusion, then test its validity on every assignment.
meaning: A propositional argument is valid when no truth assignment makes all its premises true and its conclusion false. The truth of the current conclusion is a different question. Modus ponens and modus tollens are valid patterns; affirming the consequent has a counterexample even though it can give a true conclusion in some individual cases.

definition.setting: Semantic validity of three fixed classical propositional argument patterns with two independent atomic statements.

signature.⊨: Semantic entailment from premises to conclusion.

conditions: Panel length x and width y independently range from zero to 12 cm. P means x≥6 cm and Q means y≥4 cm, with equality included.
The premises and conclusion use classical truth-functional meanings. P→Q is material implication, which does not assert a cause or an empirical size law.
A counterexample assignment must make every premise true and the conclusion false. A row with a false premise is not a counterexample to validity.

definition.domain_notes: Semantic entailment means preservation of truth across all assignments satisfying the premises. This differs from deriving a formula inside a specified syntactic proof calculus. Every allowed P/Q assignment is represented in the table.

grammar.formation_rule: Let P mean x≥6 cm and Q mean y≥4 cm. Modus ponens uses premises P→Q and P with conclusion Q. Modus tollens uses P→Q and ¬Q with conclusion ¬P. The invalid pattern affirming the consequent uses P→Q and Q with conclusion P. Enumerate all four assignments: validity means there is no row with all premises true and conclusion false.

prompts.prompt: Can a valid pattern have a false current conclusion?
prompts.answer: Yes, if its premises are not all true on that assignment. Validity excludes only true-premises/false-conclusion cases.
Take P=False and Q=True. Then P→Q and Q are both true while the conclusion P is false.
